headline: Debris Cascade Shreds Three Constellations as the Blame Fight Reaches Orbit
body: A collision in low Earth orbit, a crowded zone a few hundred kilometers up, set off a cascade of crashes that destroyed satellite networks across three countries. It began when Mexico's ground team fired a short burst of its engines to dodge debris, but the maneuver instead sent an old object straight into the debris field. India blames an Indonesian satellite that was never safely removed from orbit at the end of its life; Indonesia blames a decades-old Indian rocket part still circling above, so both now blame Mexico instead. Luxembourg, whose satellite-insurance business depended on the destroyed fleet, wants payment from whichever country is finally declared the launching state, held responsible under international law for the object.
role_amplifier: India and Indonesia (each blaming the other to escape liability)
forces: outer space & orbital domain; insurance & liability; attribution
note: Kessler-style cascade is escalated past the record, but every mechanism is sound: orbital debris liability runs through the 1972 Liability Convention, which requires a named launching state, and space insurance genuinely cannot pay without attribution. Luxembourg is a real satellite and space-resources jurisdiction. Collision-avoidance burns are routinely coordinated from third-party ground stations.

headline: Famine Threshold Crossed, Activating a Duty No Signatory Will Accept
body: Sudan has been classified as experiencing famine, the most severe stage on the hunger scale. That should trigger a standby relief compact, a rescue plan a group of countries agreed to in advance. Denmark, which decides this year when the plan takes effect, says the duty is shared jointly among every country that signed it and refuses to name one country to lead. Mexico, assigned to fly in the first aid, says its own duty only begins once funding is actually paid in, and none of the signing countries have done so. Chad, sheltering two million people who crossed its border, says its supplies are running out and needs a safe route for aid opened within days.
role_amplifier: Denmark (protecting a collective-duty reading of the compact)
forces: humanitarian aid; food systems & famine; migration & displacement
note: Could be tomorrow. IPC Phase 5 famine classification is a real threshold mechanism, Sudan's famine and Chad's refugee load are documented, and threshold-triggered standby financing exists in practice. Only the specific compact and Mexico's first-mover designation are invented. The failure mode — everyone agrees, no one is bound — is the standing critique of trigger-based humanitarian finance.

headline: Rival Seed Registries Split the Genome and Force Growers to Pick a Standard
body: Crop genetic data, the genetic information recorded for each plant variety, used to sit in one shared system; now two rival registries, or databases, are competing to become the standard. One is run by a Dutch industry group; the other, led by Ethiopia, treats genetic sequences as property belonging to the country that grew them. Mexico holds the world's largest maize and wheat seed collections, so whichever registry it joins will likely become the standard through sheer size alone, and both are already offering it a seat on their governing boards. Peru, caught in between while negotiating royalties for potato varieties it developed, finds that buyers now demand paperwork filed in their preferred system before they will pay.
forces: food systems & seeds; cultural sovereignty; technology & standard-setting
note: Digital sequence information and benefit-sharing is a live, unresolved fight under the Nagoya Protocol and the CBD. The Netherlands is the world's largest seed exporter, Ethiopia is a Vavilov center of crop diversity, Peru anchors potato genetic diversity, and Mexico is the center of origin for maize and hosts the largest maize and wheat collections. Only the two named registries are invented.

headline: Insolvent Miner Abandons a Live Seabed Plume With No One in Custody
body: A company doing deep-sea mining, digging minerals from the ocean floor, went bankrupt mid-operation, leaving its equipment on the seafloor while stirred-up sediment still drifted through the water above. A Mexican research ship towed the abandoned vessel to keep it from running aground, and under salvage law, where rescuing a ship can grant ownership of it, that single act may now make Mexico its unlikely legal owner. Nauru, which had backed the firm's licence to mine, says its duty ended when the firm collapsed. Liberia, where the ship is registered, says its duty ended once the vessel was seized. Belgium, where the parent company was legally based, calls the whole mess everyone's problem.
role_amplifier: Belgium (invoking collective obligation to avoid its own)
forces: resource extraction; infrastructure; territorial control & sovereignty
note: Commercial-scale seabed mining is not yet operating, so the event is escalated — but the mechanics are real. Nauru genuinely sponsors a deep-sea mining contractor and triggered the ISA two-year rule; sponsoring-state liability is defined by the 2011 ITLOS advisory opinion; Liberia is a major open registry; Belgium hosts a leading seabed-mining firm; Mexico has backed a precautionary pause. Salvage creating custody is ordinary maritime law.

headline: One Museum Loan Could Void Every Colonial Acquisition Behind It
body: An Austrian court is about to rule on a case that looks small but carries enormous consequences: whether a feathered headdress lent to a Mexican museum for one exhibition must be returned, or whether the loan itself transferred title, full legal ownership, to Mexico. Mexico refuses to guarantee it would return the piece, so the Austrian museum that lent it now will not ship it back. The object itself matters less than the legal reasoning behind the ruling. Nigeria and Greece have both filed formal arguments with the court, because if judges decide that objects taken during the colonial era were never lawfully owned in the first place, that reasoning could be used against museums across Europe.
role_harmed: Austria's museum sector (exposure to the template)
role_amplifier: Nigeria and Greece (unrelated restitution claims riding the ruling)
forces: cultural sovereignty; recognition & legitimacy; territorial control & sovereignty
note: The Vienna headdress attributed to Moctezuma is real and Mexico has sought it for decades; Austria has refused on conservation grounds. Benin Bronzes and the Parthenon Marbles are live claims whose advocates genuinely watch each other's rulings. The invented element is a court reaching the title question through a loan dispute — a plausible route, since loan agreements do turn on who holds title.

countries: Mexico; Japan; Republic of Korea; Australia
headline: Enrichment Freeze Stalls Over Which Government Ships First
body: Japan and the Republic of Korea have both started enriching uranium, boosting the concentration of one uranium type until it can fuel reactors or, at higher levels, weapons, and a phased freeze between them has stalled over a simple question: who moves first? Whichever country ships its material out first gives up a strategic safeguard, while the other keeps the technical ability to build more later without ever using it. Australia will not supply fresh fuel to either country until both act. Mexico, whose reactors depend on the same shared fuel bank now receiving these shipments, demands it stay stocked through its own scheduled refuelling window, or it will buy fuel elsewhere.
role_holder: Japan and Republic of Korea (each holds material and the first-mover risk)
role_amplifier: Mexico (unrelated fuel-supply side-stake widening a security dispute)
forces: nuclear materials & proliferation; military alliances & defense; energy
note: Latent enrichment capability, hedging, and sequencing distrust are the core mechanics of every real freeze negotiation, including the JCPOA. Japan holds a large plutonium stockpile and full fuel-cycle capability; Korean enrichment is a recurring domestic demand; Australia holds the largest uranium reserves and imposes strict end-use conditions; Mexico's Tlatelolco leadership and Laguna Verde reactors make its fuel interest real. The programs themselves are counterfactual.

headline: Seized Smuggling Ledger Names Officials and Nobody Will Publish It
body: Mexico has opened a criminal case against a Dutch foundation, hoping a court will force it to release a ledger, a written record of payments, recovered from a smuggling network that moved people across the Mediterranean Sea. The ledger names sitting officials in four countries who received secret payments, but the foundation refuses to release it unless the two witnesses who supplied it are first relocated somewhere safe. Italy says it could formally charge its named officials within days of receiving the names, and calls the delay an illegal block on justice. Nigeria, meanwhile, wants the pages naming its own officials kept secret until after its elections.
note: Every element is documented practice: Nigerian-network trafficking through Libya into Italy, Italian prosecutions that depend on cooperating witnesses, NGO custody of leaked financial records with source-protection conditions, and prosecutions of investigators under data-protection and state-secrets law. Only the specific ledger and the four-way configuration are invented.

headline: A Single Porcine Trace Voids a Certifier and a Year of Exports With It
body: Port inspectors in Malaysia tested a beef shipment carrying Mexican halal certification, the official seal confirming food follows Islamic dietary rules that forbid pork, and found pig DNA inside the meat. Malaysia withdrew its recognition of the certifier, the group that had approved the meat as halal, so every shipment it had approved that year was cancelled, not just the one batch that failed. Argentina's meat processors quickly covered the cancelled orders at a higher price, while Egypt is now checking whether beef from the same certifier entered its own supply chain too. Mexico's regulator insists the contamination happened later, inside a Malaysian refrigerated warehouse, and wants the samples back for independent testing.
forces: religion & sacred geography; food systems; trade & shipping
note: Malaysia's JAKIM certification is the de facto global halal standard and its recognition can be withdrawn from a foreign certifier, invalidating that certifier's output wholesale. Halal fraud cases involving undeclared porcine material are documented. Argentina is a major halal-certified beef exporter and Egypt a major beef importer requiring certification. Mexican halal beef certification for Asian markets is small but real.
